title: Five Great Novels (including A Scanner Darkly)
author: Philip K. Dick
card_summary: An omnibus volume collecting five Philip K. Dick novels, including A Scanner Darkly and likely The Three Stigmata of Palmer Eldritch alongside other major works. A Scanner Darkly, published in 1977, is Dick's semi-autobiographical novel about drug addiction set in a near-future surveillance state.
page_summary:
Five Great Novels is a collected omnibus edition of major Philip K. Dick novels. Although the filename references The Three Stigmata of Palmer Eldritch, the text excerpt opens with A Scanner Darkly (1977), Dick's semi-autobiographical novel about drug addiction and surveillance in a near-future Orange County, California.

The excerpt begins with acknowledgments referencing Joseph E. Bogen's "The Other Side of the Brain" from the Bulletin of the Los Angeles Neurological Societies (July 1969) and Michael S. Gazzaniga's "The Split Brain in Man" from Scientific American (August 1967), reflecting the novel's engagement with neuroscience and divided consciousness. Poetry from Heinrich Heine and references to Goethe's Faust and Beethoven's Fidelio are also credited.

The opening scene introduces a man standing all day shaking bugs from his hair that a doctor insists do not exist, immediately establishing the novel's central themes of perceptual unreliability, drug-induced psychosis, and the dissolution of identity. A Scanner Darkly is widely regarded as one of Dick's finest achievements, drawing directly on his own experiences in the drug culture of 1970s Southern California.

## A SCANNER DARKLY 1 

Once a guy stood all day shaking bugs from his hair. The doctor told him there were no bugs in his hair. After he had taken a shower for eight hours, standing under hot water hour after hour suffering the pain of the bugs, he got out and dried himself, and he still had bugs in his hair; in fact, he had bugs all over him. A month later he had bugs in his lungs. Having nothing else to do or think about, he began to work out theoretically the life cycle of the bugs, and, with the aid of the _Britannica_, try to determine specifically which bugs they were. They now filled his house. He read about many different kinds and finally noticed bugs outdoors, so he concluded they were aphids. After that decision came to his mind it never changed, no matter what other people told him . . . like "Aphids don't bite people." 

They said that to him because the endless biting of the bugs kept him in torment. At the 7-11 grocery store, part of a chain spread out over most of California, he bought spray cans of Raid and Black Flag and Yard Guard. First he sprayed the house, then himself. The Yard Guard seemed to work the best. As to the theoretical side, he perceived three stages in the cycle of the bugs. First, they were carried to him to contaminate him by what he called Carrier-people, which were people who didn't understand their role in distributing the bugs. During that stage the bugs had no jaws or mandibles (he learned that word during his weeks of scholarly research, an unusually bookish occupation for a guy who worked at the Handy Brake and Tire place relining people's brake drums). The Carrier-people therefore felt nothing. He used to sit in the far corner of his living room watching different Carrier-people enter--most of them people he'd known for a while, but some new to him--covered with the aphids in this particular nonbiting stage. He'd sort of smile to himself, because he knew that the person was being used by the bugs and wasn't hip to it. 

"What are you grinning about, Jerry?" they'd say. He'd just smile.
